title: King Fernando of Castile dies at fifty-nine, two months before the Emperor's declaration. His son Pedro, twenty-three, takes the throne

The Emperor declares war on Castile under the Reconquest of Iberia. Portugal, the Pope with his vassals Faenza and Siena, and Andorra stand with the young King Pedro; the four ṭāʾifas, the Moors of Fās with their vassals and the Mamlūks with theirs stand with the Emperor

ourSide: Morocco and its vassals (Tafilalt, Touat, Tlemcen)

title: The first battles. Castile's great army, some 24,300 men, comes down on the small armies of the ṭāʾifas around Sigüenza, beyond the Aragonese border: Aragon's 1,840 fall back, and Valencia's 1,740 are caught and engaged on 9 August

Through August and September the Emperor's 17,650 chase the Castilian host north along the Aragonese border, from Calatayud toward the Ebro and Tudela, with the Catalan army of 7,100 and Aragon's 1,840 shadowing it on the other flank
source: Trent's account and map screenshot, August–September 1394

title: The ambush at Banbalūna. The Castilians, pursuing an Aragonese army of 8,900 into the hills of Navarre, find the Emperor across their path at Pamplona: their pursuit is cut off and their host of 24,200 is beaten, 2,440 lost for 1,450 of ours. Castile retreats in haste
source: Trent's account and battle screens, 9–12 October 1394

title: After Pamplona the Castilian host, still 21,700 strong, comes back south out of Navarre toward the Ebro. The Emperor's 16,200 shadow it from the west, the Catalan 7,100 wait on the Aragonese side, and Mamlūk contingents of 2,300 and 700 stand among the Castilian forts of Soria

The Battle of Ejea de los Caballeros. The Emperor catches the Castilian host on the plain of the Cinco Villas, on ground that favours the defender, and Agustín Arce, Grand Master of Alcántara and the best general Castile has, holds it for nine days. It matters not: when it ends, 10,800 Castilians are dead or scattered against 4,660 of ours, and the war swings by twenty points
